Analytic solutions for censored delay distributions

Source: vignettes/analytic-solutions.Rmd
analytic-solutions.Rmd

1 Introduction

1.1 What are we going to do in this vignette

In this vignette, we’ll derive the analytic solutions for the primary censored delay distributions for a range of commonly used distributions.

  1. Examine the case of exponentially tilted primary event times
  2. Analyse the uniform primary event time case (\(r=0\))
  3. Explore general partial expectation and its role in solving equation (3.1)
  4. Provide specific analytic solutions for distributions where the partial expectation can be reduced to an analytic expression
  5. Derive transform based solutions for the exponentially tilted primary event time with exponential, gamma, normal, Weibull and generalised gamma delays, and with the lognormal delay by quadrature or series
  6. Derive a series solution for a truncated Gumbel primary event time with a normal delay from the same transforms, and find where it is accurate

2 Analytic solutions for exponentially tilted primary event times

In epidemiological analysis, it is common for primary events to occur at exponentially increasing or decreasing rates, for example, incidence of new infections in an epidemic. In this case, the distribution of the primary event time within its censoring window is biased by the exponential growth or decay[1] (i.e. for exponential growth, the event time will more likely to be closer to the end of the censoring window and vice versa for decay). If we assume a reference uniform distribution within a primary censoring window \([k, k + w_P)\) then the distribution of the primary event time within the censoring window is the exponential tilted uniform distribution:

\[ f_P(t) \propto \exp(r t) \mathbb{1}_{[k, k + w_P]}(t). \]

In this case, the distribution function for \(C_P\), that is the length of time left in the primary censor window after the primary event time, is given by:

\[ F_{C_P}(p; r) = { 1 - \exp(-r p) \over 1 - \exp(-r w_P)}, \qquad p \in [0, w_P]. \tag{2.1} \] Note that taking the limit \(\lim_r \rightarrow 0\) in equation (2.1) gives the uniform distribution function \(F_{C_P}(p, 0) = p / w_P\).

In the following, it is convenient to use a (linear) difference operator defined as:

\[ \Delta_{w}f(t) = f(t + w) - f(t). \]

3 Uniform primary event time (\(r=0\))

Applying a uniform primary event time distribution to equation 3.1 from “Why it works” gives:

\[ Q_{S_+}(t) = Q_T(t + w_P) + { 1 \over w_P} \int_0^{w_P} f_T(t+p) p~ dp. \]

This is analytically solvable whenever the upper distribution function of \(T\) is known and the mean of \(T\) is analytically solvable from its integral definition.

In each case considered below it is easier to change the integration variable:

\[ \begin{aligned} Q_{S_+}(t) &= Q_T(t + w_P) + { 1 \over w_P} \int_t^{t+w_P} f_T(z) (z-t)~ dz \\ &= Q_T(t + w_P) + { 1 \over w_P} \Big[ \int_t^{t+w_P} f_T(z) z~ dz - t \Delta_{w_P}F_T(t) \Big]. \end{aligned} \tag{3.1} \]

3.1 General partial expectation

Note that for any distribution with an analytically available distribution function \(F_T\) equation (3.1) can be solved so long as the partial expectation

\[ \int_t^{t+w_P} f_T(z) z~ dz \tag{3.2} \]

can be reduced to an analytic expression.

The insight here is that this will be possible for any distribution where the average of the distribution can be calculated analytically, which includes commonly used non-negative distributions such as the Gamma, Log-Normal and Weibull distributions.

3.2 General discrete censored delay distribution

First, we note that equation 3.3 from “Why it works” can be written using the difference operator: \(f_n = -\Delta_1 Q_{S_+}(n-1)\). We can insert this expression into equation (3.1) to give the discrete censored delay distribution for uniformly distributed primary event times:

\[ \begin{aligned} f_n &= \Delta_1\Big[(n-1) \Delta_1F_T(n-1)\Big] - \Delta_1Q_T(n) - \Delta_1\Big[ \int_{n-1}^n f_T(z) z ~dz \Big] \\ &= (n+1)F_T(n+1) + (n-1)F_T(n-1) - 2nF_T(n) - \Delta_1\Big[ \int_{n-1}^n f_T(z) z ~dz \Big]. \end{aligned} \tag{3.3} \]

We now consider some specific delay distributions.

3.3 Gamma distributed delay times

The Gamma distribution has the density function:

\[ f_T(z;k, \theta) = {1 \over \Gamma(k) \theta^k} z^{k-1} \exp(-z/\theta). \] Where \(\Gamma\) is the Gamma function.

The Gamma distribution has the distribution function:

\[ \begin{aligned} F_T(z;k, \theta) &= {\gamma(k, z/\theta) \over \Gamma(k)}, \qquad z\geq 0,\\ F_T(z;k, \theta) &= 0, \qquad z < 0. \end{aligned} \] Where \(\gamma\) is the lower incomplete gamma function.

3.3.1 Gamma partial expectation

We know that the full expectation of the Gamma distribution is \(\mathbb{E}[T] = k\theta\), which can be calculated as a standard integral. Doing the same integral for the partial expectation gives:

\[ \begin{aligned} \int_t^{t+w_P} f_T(z) z~ dz &= {1 \over \Gamma(k) \theta^k} \int_t^{t+w_P} \mathbb{1}(z \geq 0) z z^{k-1} \exp(-z/\theta)~dz \\ &= {\Gamma(k+1) \theta^{k+1} \over \Gamma(k) \theta^k} {1 \over \Gamma(k+1) \theta^{k+1}} \int_t^{t+w_P} \mathbb{1}(z \geq 0) z^{k} \exp(-z/\theta)~dz\\ &= k\theta \Delta_{w_P} F_T(t; k + 1, \theta). \end{aligned} \tag{3.4} \]

3.3.2 Survival function of \(S_{+}\) for Gamma distribution

By substituting equation (3.4) into equation (3.3) we can solve for the survival function of \(S_+\) in terms of analytically available functions:

\[ Q_{S_+}(t; k, \theta) = Q_T(t + w_P; k, \theta) + { 1 \over w_P} \big[ k \theta \Delta_{w_P}F_T(t; k+1, \theta) - t \Delta_{w_P}F_T(t; k, \theta) \big]. \tag{3.5} \]

3.3.3 CDF form of \(S_{+}\) for Gamma distribution

Rearranging equation (3.5) via \(F_{S_+} = 1 - Q_{S_+}\) gives the equivalent CDF-direct form

\[ F_{S_+}(d; k, \theta) = \frac{1}{w_P}\Big[ d\, F_T(d; k, \theta) - q\, F_T(q; k, \theta) - k\theta\big( F_T(d; k{+}1, \theta) - F_T(q; k{+}1, \theta) \big) \Big], \]

where \(q = \max(d - w_P, 0)\).

3.3.4 Gamma discrete censored delay distribution

By substituting (3.5) into (3.3) we get the discrete censored delay distribution in terms of analytically available functions: \[ \begin{aligned} f_n &= (n+1) F_T(n+1; k, \theta) + (n-1) F_T(n-1; k, \theta) - 2 n F_T(n; k, \theta) - k \theta \Delta_1^{(2)}F_T(n-1; k+1, \theta)\\ &= (n+1) F_T(n+1; k, \theta) + (n-1) F_T(n-1; k, \theta) - 2 n F_T(n; k, \theta) \\ &+ k \theta \Big( 2 F_T(n; k+1, \theta) - F_T(n-1; k+1, \theta) - F_T(n+1; k+1,\theta) \Big) \qquad n = 0, 1, \dots. \end{aligned} \]

Which was also found by Cori et al[2].

3.4 Log-Normal distribution

The Log-Normal distribution has the density function:

\[ \begin{aligned} f_T(z;\mu, \sigma) &= {1 \over z \sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left( - {(\log(z) - \mu)^2 \over 2 \sigma^2} \right)\\ F_T(z;\mu, \sigma) &= 0, \qquad z < 0. \end{aligned} \] And distribution function:

\[ F_T(z;\mu, \sigma) = \Phi\left( {\log(z) - \mu \over \sigma} \right). \] Where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function.

3.4.1 Log-Normal partial expectation

We know that the full expectation of the Log-Normal distribution is \(\mathbb{E}[T] = e^{\mu + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2}\), which can be calculated by integration with the integration substitution \(y = (\ln z - \mu) / \sigma\). This has transformation Jacobian:

\[ \frac{dz}{dy} = \sigma e^{\sigma y + \mu}. \]

Doing the same integral for the partial expectation, and using the same integration substitution gives:

\[ \begin{aligned} \int_t^{t+w_P} z~ f_T(z; \mu, \sigma) dz &= {1 \over \sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} \int_t^{t+w_P} \mathbb{1}(z \geq 0) \exp\left( - {(\log(z) - \mu)^2 \over 2 \sigma^2} \right) dz \\ &= {1 \over \sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{(\ln t - \mu)/\sigma}^{(\ln(t+w_P) - \mu)/\sigma} e^{\sigma y + \mu} e^{-y^2/2} dy\\ &= {e^{\mu + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2} \over \sqrt{2 \pi} } \int_{(\ln t - \mu)/\sigma}^{(\ln(t+w_P) - \mu)/\sigma} e^{-(y- \sigma)^2/2} dy \\ &= e^{\mu + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2} \Big[\Phi\Big({\ln(t+w_P) - \mu \over \sigma} - \sigma\Big) - \Phi\Big({\ln(t) - \mu \over \sigma} - \sigma\Big) \Big]\\ &= e^{\mu + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2} \Delta_{w_P}F_T(t; \mu + \sigma^2, \sigma). \end{aligned} \tag{3.6} \]

3.4.2 Survival function of \(S_{+}\) for Log-Normal distribution

By substituting equation (3.6) into equation (3.3) we can solve for the survival function of \(S_+\) in terms of analytically available functions:

\[ Q_{S+}(t ;\mu, \sigma) = Q_T(t + w_P;\mu, \sigma) + { 1 \over w_P} \Big[ e^{\mu + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2} \Delta_{w_P}F_T(t; \mu + \sigma^2, \sigma) - t\Delta_{w_P}F_T(t; \mu, \sigma) \Big] \]

3.4.3 CDF form of \(S_{+}\) for Log-Normal distribution

Applying \(F_{S_+} = 1 - Q_{S_+}\) to the preceding survival form gives the equivalent CDF-direct form

\[ F_{S_+}(d; \mu, \sigma) = \frac{1}{w_P}\Big[ d\, F_T(d; \mu, \sigma) - q\, F_T(q; \mu, \sigma) - e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}\big( F_T(d; \mu{+}\sigma^2, \sigma) - F_T(q; \mu{+}\sigma^2, \sigma) \big) \Big], \]

where \(q = \max(d - w_P, 0)\).

3.4.4 Log-Normal discrete censored delay distribution

By substituting (3.6) into (3.3) we get the discrete censored delay distribution in terms of analytically available functions:

\[ \begin{aligned} f_n &= (n+1) F_T(n+1; \mu, \sigma) + (n-1) F_T(n-1; \mu, \sigma) - 2 n F_T(n; \mu, \sigma) \\ &- e^{\mu + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2} \Delta_1^{(2)}F_T(n-1;\mu + \sigma^2, \sigma) \\ &= (n+1) F_T(n+1; \mu, \sigma) + (n-1) F_T(n-1; \mu, \sigma) - 2 n F_T(n; \mu, \sigma) \\ &+ e^{\mu + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2} \Big( 2 F_T(n; \mu + \sigma^2, \sigma) - F_T(n+1; \mu + \sigma^2, \sigma) - F_T(n-1; \mu + \sigma^2, \sigma) \Big)\qquad n = 0, 1, \dots. \end{aligned} \]

3.5 Weibull distribution

The Weibull distribution has the density function:

\[ f_T(z;\lambda,k) = \begin{cases} \frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{z}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}e^{-(z/\lambda)^{k}}, & z\geq0 ,\\ 0, & z<0, \end{cases} \] And distribution function:

\[ F_T(z;\lambda,k))=\begin{cases}1 - e^{-(z/\lambda)^k}, & z\geq0,\\ 0, & z<0.\end{cases} \] Where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function.

3.5.1 Weibull partial expectation

We know that the full expectation of the Weibull distribution is \(\mathbb{E}[T] = \lambda \Gamma(1 + 1/k)\), which can be calculated by integration using the integration substitution \(y = (z / \lambda)^k\), which has transformation Jacobian:

\[ \frac{dz}{dy} = \frac{\lambda}{k}y^{1/k - 1}. \]

Doing the same integral for the partial expectation, and using the same integration substitution gives:

\[ \begin{aligned} \int_{t}^{t+w_P} z~ f_T(z; \lambda,k) dz &= \int_t^{t+w_P} \mathbb{1}(z \geq 0) \frac{kz}{\lambda}\left(\frac{z}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}e^{-(z/\lambda)^{k}} dz \\ &= k\int_t^{t+w_P} \mathbb{1}(z \geq 0) \left(\frac{z}{\lambda}\right)^{k}e^{-(z/\lambda)^{k}} dz \\ &= \lambda k \int_{(t / \lambda)^k}^{((t + w_P) / \lambda)^k} \mathbb{1}(y \geq 0) y y^{1/k - 1} e^{-y} dy \\ &= \lambda\int_{(t / \lambda)^k}^{((t + w_P) / \lambda)^k} \mathbb{1}(y \geq 0) y^{1/k} e^{-y} dy\\ &= \lambda \Delta_{w_P} g(t; \lambda,k) \end{aligned} \tag{3.7} \]

Where

\[ g(t; \lambda, k) = \gamma\left(1 + 1/k, \left({t\vee 0 \over \lambda}\right)^k\right) = \frac{1}{k}\gamma\left(1/k, \left({t\vee 0 \over \lambda}\right)^k\right) - \frac{t}{\lambda}\exp\left(-\left({t\vee 0 \over \lambda}\right)^k\right) \] is a reparametrisation of the lower incomplete gamma function. Note that the \(\vee\) operator \(t \vee 0 = \text{max}(0, t)\) comes into the expression due to \(\mathbb{1}(y \geq 0)\) term in the integrand.

3.6 Survival function of \(S_{+}\) for Weibull distribution

By substituting equation (3.7) into equation (3.3) we can solve for the survival function of \(S_+\) in terms of analytically available functions:

\[ Q_{S+}(t ;\lambda,k) = Q_T(t + w_P; \lambda,k) + { 1 \over w_P} \Big[ \lambda \Delta_{w_P} g(t; \lambda,k) - t\Delta_{w_P}F_T(t; \lambda,k)\Big]. \]

3.6.1 CDF form of \(S_{+}\) for Weibull distribution

Applying \(F_{S_+} = 1 - Q_{S_+}\) to the preceding survival form gives the equivalent CDF-direct form

\[ F_{S_+}(d; \lambda, k) = \frac{1}{w_P}\Big[ d\, F_T(d; \lambda, k) - q\, F_T(q; \lambda, k) - \lambda\big( g(d; \lambda, k) - g(q; \lambda, k) \big) \Big], \]

where \(q = \max(d - w_P, 0)\) and \(g\) is as defined in equation (3.7).

3.6.2 Weibull discrete censored delay distribution

By substituting (3.7) into (3.3) we get the discrete censored delay distribution in terms of analytically available functions:

\[ \begin{aligned} f_n &= (n+1)F_T(n+1) + (n-1)F_T(n-1) - 2nF_T(n) - \Delta_1\Big[ \int_{n-1}^n f_T(z) z ~dz \Big] \\ &= (n+1)F_T(n+1) + (n-1)F_T(n-1) - 2nF_T(n) - \lambda \Delta_1^{(2)} g(n-1; \lambda,k) \\ &= (n+1)F_T(n+1) + (n-1)F_T(n-1) - 2nF_T(n) \\ &+ \lambda [2 g(n; \lambda,k) - g(n+1; \lambda,k) - g(n-1; \lambda,k)] \qquad n = 0, 1, \dots. \end{aligned} \]

Which was also found by Cori et al[2].

3.7 Generalised gamma distribution

The generalised gamma distribution, in the parameterisation of Stacy[3] as implemented by flexsurv::pgengamma.orig(), has the density function:

\[ f_T(z; a, \theta, k) = \begin{cases} \frac{a}{\Gamma(k)\theta}\left(\frac{z}{\theta}\right)^{a k-1}e^{-(z/\theta)^{a}}, & z\geq0 ,\\ 0, & z<0, \end{cases} \] And distribution function:

\[ F_T(z; a, \theta, k) =\begin{cases} {\gamma\left(k, (z/\theta)^a\right) \over \Gamma(k)}, & z\geq0,\\ 0, & z<0.\end{cases} \] Where \(\gamma\) is the lower incomplete gamma function. The Gamma distribution is the special case \(a = 1\) and the Weibull distribution is the special case \(k = 1\).

3.7.1 Generalised gamma partial expectation

Using the integration substitution \(y = (z / \theta)^a\) as for the Weibull distribution, the full expectation is \(\mathbb{E}[T] = \theta \Gamma(k + 1/a) / \Gamma(k)\). Doing the same integral for the partial expectation gives:

\[ \begin{aligned} \int_{t}^{t+w_P} z~ f_T(z; a, \theta, k) dz &= \frac{\theta}{\Gamma(k)} \int_{(t / \theta)^a}^{((t + w_P) / \theta)^a} \mathbb{1}(y \geq 0) y^{k + 1/a - 1} e^{-y} dy\\ &= \theta \frac{\Gamma(k + 1/a)}{\Gamma(k)} \Delta_{w_P} F_T(t; a, \theta, k + 1/a). \end{aligned} \tag{3.8} \]

That is, the partial expectation distribution is the generalised gamma distribution with \(k\) replaced by \(k + 1/a\). For \(a = 1\) this recovers equation (3.4) and for \(k = 1\) it recovers equation (3.7).

3.7.2 Survival function of \(S_{+}\) for generalised gamma distribution

By substituting equation (3.8) into equation (3.1) we can solve for the survival function of \(S_+\) in terms of analytically available functions:

\[ Q_{S_+}(t; a, \theta, k) = Q_T(t + w_P; a, \theta, k) + { 1 \over w_P} \Big[ \theta \frac{\Gamma(k + 1/a)}{\Gamma(k)} \Delta_{w_P}F_T(t; a, \theta, k + 1/a) - t \Delta_{w_P}F_T(t; a, \theta, k) \Big]. \tag{3.9} \]

3.7.3 CDF form of \(S_{+}\) for generalised gamma distribution

Rearranging equation (3.9) via \(F_{S_+} = 1 - Q_{S_+}\) gives the equivalent CDF-direct form

\[ F_{S_+}(d; a, \theta, k) = \frac{1}{w_P}\Big[ d\, F_T(d; a, \theta, k) - q\, F_T(q; a, \theta, k) - \theta \frac{\Gamma(k + 1/a)}{\Gamma(k)} \big( F_T(d; a, \theta, k + 1/a) - F_T(q; a, \theta, k + 1/a) \big) \Big], \]

where \(q = \max(d - w_P, 0)\). This is the form implemented in pcens_cdf() and in the Stan function primarycensored_gengamma_uniform_lcdf(). The discrete censored delay distribution follows from equation (3.3) exactly as for the Gamma distribution, with \(k\theta F_T(\cdot; k + 1, \theta)\) replaced by \(\theta \frac{\Gamma(k + 1/a)}{\Gamma(k)} F_T(\cdot; a, \theta, k + 1/a)\).

4 Transform based solutions for exponentially tilted primary event times

The uniform solutions above need the CDF and the partial expectation of the delay. For an exponentially tilted primary event time both are special cases of the truncated exponential-moment transform of the delay density,

\[ T_f(\xi; \tau) = \int_{-\infty}^{\tau} e^{\xi u} f_T(u) ~du, \]

where the lower limit is 0 for delays on the non-negative reals. The CDF is \(F_T(\tau) = T_f(0; \tau)\). A new delay distribution is supported by adding a transform (.pcens_tilt_transform() in R and log_tilt_transform_pair() in Stan).

With the density \(f_P(z) = r e^{r z} / (e^{r w_P} - 1)\) on \([0, w_P]\) of the primary event time, which is the dexpgrowth() distribution, write \(q = d - w_P\) and \(J(x) = T_f(-r; x)\). Changing variables and integrating by parts as for the uniform case gives

\[ F_{S_+}(d) = F_T(q) + \frac{e^{r d} \{J(d) - J(q)\} - \{F_T(d) - F_T(q)\}}{e^{r w_P} - 1}, \tag{4.1} \]

with \(F_T(x) = J(x) = 0\) for \(x \leq 0\) for delays on the non-negative reals. Every term depends on \(d\) or on \(q\) alone, so primarycensored_analytical_lcdf_vectorized() computes the terms once per integer delay and uses them for the two windows that share the endpoint.

4.1 Closed form transforms

For \(\xi = -r\) the closed form transforms are as follows.

  • Exponential with rate \(\lambda\): \(T_f(\xi; \tau) = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda - \xi}\{1 - e^{-(\lambda - \xi)\tau}\}\).
  • Gamma with shape \(\alpha\) and rate \(\lambda\): \(T_f(\xi; \tau) = \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - \xi}\right)^{\alpha} P(\alpha, (\lambda - \xi)\tau)\) where \(P\) is the regularised lower incomplete gamma function.
  • Normal with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\): \(T_f(\xi; \tau) = e^{\xi\mu + \xi^2\sigma^2/2}\,\Phi\left(\frac{\tau - \mu - \xi\sigma^2}{\sigma}\right)\), with no lower limit at 0. As the delay has support on the reals, the terms at \(q < 0\) are not zero and the solution also holds for \(d < 0\).

Differences between the two endpoints are taken from the lower or the upper tail transforms, whichever has the smaller ratio of the subtracted term to the first. All terms are evaluated on the log scale.

4.2 Incomplete gamma series transforms

The Weibull and the generalised gamma are in the Stacy family, with CDF \(F_T(x) = P(k, (x / \theta)^a)\) for the shape \(a\), scale \(\theta\) and \(k\) of flexsurv::pgengamma.orig(), where \(k = 1\) is the Weibull. Expanding \(e^{\xi u}\) and integrating term by term gives

\[ T_f(\xi; \tau) = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \frac{(\xi \theta)^n}{n!} \frac{\Gamma(k + n / a)}{\Gamma(k)} P\left(k + n / a, (\tau / \theta)^a\right). \]

For \(\xi < 0\) the terms alternate in sign and cancel. The sum of their absolute values is \(T_f(|\xi|; \tau)\), and the series is used where this is less than \(10^5\) times the sum. The series has no upper tail form, so differences between endpoints come from the lower transform and lose about \(10^{-16}\) times the size of the terms over \(e^{r w_P} - 1\). In R the numerical path is used where that size is more than \(10^5\) times the smaller of the CDF and its survival function, which is in the upper tail. In Stan the ODE is used where the size is more than \(10^5\), as the ODE has a larger absolute error below that. In the vectorised Stan PMF the ODE values are shifted by their difference from the series value at the delay before the switch, so the PMF across the switch is a difference of ODE values. The numerical path is also used where the terms cancel too much, and where \(|\xi| \tau \geq 400\).

4.3 Lognormal delay by quadrature or series

The lognormal has no closed form transform. With \(u = e^{\mu + \sigma z}\) and \(z_\tau = (\log \tau - \mu) / \sigma\),

\[ T_f(\xi; \tau) = \int_{-\infty}^{z_\tau} e^{\xi e^{\mu + \sigma z}} \phi(z) ~dz, \]

where \(\phi\) is the standard normal density. The method depends on the sign of \(\xi = -r\).

  • For \(r > 0\), \(\xi < 0\), the log of the integrand \(\ell(z) = -r e^{\mu + \sigma z} - z^2 / 2\) is concave with one mode, \(z_0 = -W_0(r \sigma^2 e^\mu) / \sigma\), where \(W_0\) is the principal branch of the Lambert W function. The integrand is below \(e^{-40}\) of its peak beyond limits set from the curvature and the decay of the tilt. The total is integrated by two 32 point Gauss-Legendre panels that meet at the mode, once for all the points of a call. For a point left of the mode the lower transform is one panel that ends at the point. For a point right of the mode the upper transform is one panel that starts at the point. The other transform is the difference from the total, which is at least the mass on the other side of the mode, so it does not cancel. Each panel is split into ceiling(sigma / 1.8) equal panels for a larger \(\sigma\), which keeps the CDF accurate to about \(10^{-9}\) to \(\sigma = 15\).
  • For \(r < 0\), \(\xi > 0\), the transform is the series \(\sum_{k \geq 0} \xi^k m_k(\tau) / k!\) in the partial moments \(m_k(\tau) = \int_0^\tau u^k f_T(u)~du = e^{k\mu + k^2\sigma^2/2}\,\Phi(z_\tau - k\sigma)\). All terms are positive, so the sum does not cancel. Past \(k = \xi \tau\) the terms fall by at least a factor \(\xi \tau / (k + 1)\), so about \(\xi \tau + 9 \sqrt{\xi \tau} + 30\) terms are needed. The total diverges, so there is no upper transform.

The moments \(G_1\), \(G_2\) and \(G_3\) of the small tilt forms come from \(m_0\) to \(m_3\).

4.4 Admissibility

The exponential and gamma forms need \(\lambda - \xi = \lambda + r > 0\) for the tilted delay distribution to exist. Where \(\lambda + r \leq 0\) the methods use the numerical path, pcens_cdf.default() in R and the ODE in Stan. In Stan check_for_analytical_params() makes the choice from the parameters. The normal form and the series for the Weibull and the generalised gamma have no restriction. The lognormal needs that \(r \sigma^2 e^\mu\) is finite. For \(r < 0\) the series needs about \(\xi d + 9 \sqrt{\xi d} + 30\) terms at a delay \(d\), so the numerical path is used past \(|r| d\) of 200 in R and 60 in Stan, where it is faster. In Stan check_for_analytical_delay() makes this choice at each delay. The exception is a window that is wide in tilt terms, \(|r| w_P > 2\), where the numerical path is less accurate in the lower tail. The series is kept there up to 20000 terms, which is \(|r| d\) up to about 18700. For fewer than 10 quantiles in R the numerical method is used only where \(|r| w_P \leq 1\), where its error is about \(10^{-6}\).

4.5 Tilts close to zero

Equation (4.1) cancels as \(r \to 0\), and for a gamma delay loses precision in proportion to the shape. Two forms replace it, with \(G_k(t) = \int (t - u)^k f_T(u)~du\) over the support up to \(t\).

For \(|r| w_P < 10^{-2}\), or \(10^{-3}\) for delays on the reals, and \(|r| (|d| + w_P) < 0.1\), expanding the window density in \(r\) gives the uniform solution and its corrections to second order,

\[ \begin{aligned} F_{S_+}(d) = {} & \frac{G_1(d) - G_1(q)}{w_P} + r \frac{G_2(d) - w_P G_1(d) - G_2(q) - w_P G_1(q)}{2 w_P} \\ & + r^2 \frac{2 \{G_3(d) - G_3(q)\} - 3 w_P \{G_2(d) + G_2(q)\} + w_P^2 \{G_1(d) - G_1(q)\}}{12 w_P} + O\big((r w_P)^3\big). \end{aligned} \]

For a delay on the non-negative reals with \(d < w_P\), where the terms at \(q\) are zero, and \(|r| d < 5 \times 10^{-3}\), the direct form cancels as \(d \to 0\) and

\[ F_{S_+}(d) = \frac{r \{G_1(d) + r G_2(d) / 2 + r^2 G_3(d) / 6\}}{e^{r w_P} - 1} + O\big((r d)^3\big) \]

is used instead. The relative truncation errors are below \((|r| w_P)^3 / 160\) and \((|r| d)^3 / 24\), so both are below \(10^{-8}\) at these limits.

The first form subtracts terms of the size of \(|d| + w_P\), so it has a rounding error of about \(10^{-14} (|d| + w_P) / w_P \{1 + |r| (|d| + w_P)\}\). Equation (4.1) has a rounding error of about \(10^{-15} / (|r| w_P)\) at any distance from the origin. The first form has the smaller error while \(|r| (|d| + w_P)\) is below about 0.1, so equation (4.1) is used beyond that.

5 Log-logistic delays

The log-logistic distribution with shape \(k\) and scale \(\lambda\) has CDF \(F_T(x) = 1 / (1 + (x / \lambda)^{-k})\). The uniform primary needs the partial expectation \(\int_0^t u f_T(u) du = t F_T(t) r_{1/k}(A)\), where \(A = (t / \lambda)^k\) and

\[ r_a(A) = \frac{1 + A}{A^{a+1}} \int_0^A \frac{y^a}{(1 + y)^2} ~dy. \]

The ratio \(r_a(A)\) is the expectation of \((U / t)^a\) for a delay \(U\) at most \(t\), and is at most \(1 / (a + 1)\). The integral is an incomplete beta function for \(a < 1\) only, and is also a Gauss hypergeometric function, which base R does not have. The package instead evaluates \(r_a\) from three series that do not cancel.

  • For \(A \leq 1\) and \(B = A / (1 + A)\), \(r_a = (1 - B)^a \sum_m \frac{(a)_m}{m!} \frac{B^m}{a + m + 1}\).
  • For \(1 < A \leq 3\), the integral is its value at \(A = 1\), from the digamma function, plus a power series in \((A - 1) / (A + 1) \leq 1/2\).
  • For \(A > 3\), the integral is its value at \(A = 3\) plus the integral from 3 to \(A\) taken term by term in \((1 + y)^{-2} = \sum_m (-1)^m (m + 1) y^{-m-2}\).

The CDF is the difference of \(\int_0^t F_T(u) du = t F_T(t) (1 - r_{1/k}(A))\) at \(d\) and \(q\), divided by \(w_P\). This difference loses about \(4 \times 10^{-16} (1 + |\log t F_T(t)|) t F_T(t) / w_P\) of the CDF to rounding. It is used for a shape of at least 0.01. The methods use the numerical path where the bound on this error exceeds \(10^{-8}\) times the smaller of the CDF and the survival, or \(10^{-6}\) times the density of the CDF, the scale of the PMF of a unit secondary window. The bound is not taken below \(10^{-15}\) in the upper tail, the resolution of a CDF close to 1. The R and Stan functions use the same rule. The numerical path integrates the delay CDF, or the survival where the delay CDF at the mean primary event time is above a half, with a relative tolerance of \(10^{-13}\). The switch between paths makes the CDF discontinuous by about \(10^{-8}\) of the smaller tail.

The Stan parameters are [scale, shape], the order of the Stan loglogistic_cdf(), and dist_id is 29. The R methods read shape and scale, or rate, as flexsurv::pllogis() and actuar::pllogis() do.

6 Transform based solutions for truncated logistic primary event times

A truncated logistic primary event window describes an exposure probability that increases smoothly and then saturates, for example an environmental source that becomes established. With the logistic CDF \(L(z) = 1 / (1 + e^{-(z - m) / s})\), location \(m\) and scale \(s\), and \(D_L = L(w_P) - L(0)\), the density on \([0, w_P]\) is \(L'(z) / D_L\), which is the dtlogis() distribution. Changing variables and integrating by parts as for the other windows gives

\[ F_{S_+}(d) = F_T(a) + \frac{1}{D_L} \int_{a}^{d} \{L(d - u) - L(0)\} f_T(u) ~du, \quad a = d - w_P. \tag{6.1} \]

With \(p = d - u\) the primary event time, \(L(p) = 1 / (1 + x)\) with \(x = e^{-(p - m) / s}\). For \(p > m\), \(x < 1\) and \(L(p) = \sum_{n \geq 0} (-x)^n\), so the integral is a sum of the transforms \(T_f(n / s; \cdot)\) at the positive tilts \(\xi = n / s\). For \(p < m\), \(L(p) = \sum_{n \geq 1} (-1)^{n - 1} x^{-n}\) needs the negative tilts \(\xi = -n / s\). The window is split at \(p = m\), at \(u^\star = d - m\), when the location is inside it. With \(\Delta T(\xi; a, b) = T_f(\xi; b) - T_f(\xi; a)\) and \(\Delta F(a, b) = F_T(b) - F_T(a)\) the three cases are as follows.

  • For \(m < 0\) the whole window is above the location and \(\Phi = \int_a^d \{L(d - u) - L(0)\} f_T(u) du\) is \[\sum_{n \geq 1} (-1)^{n - 1} e^{n m / s} \{\Delta F(a, d) - e^{-n d / s} \Delta T(n / s; a, d)\}.\] Writing \(L(0)\) as the series and subtracting it term by term removes the constant 1 of the series, so nothing cancels when \(D_L\) is small.
  • For \(0 \leq m < w_P\) the part above the location gives \[\Phi_P = \sum_{n \geq 0} (-1)^n e^{-n (d - m) / s} \Delta T(n / s; a, u^\star) - L(0) \Delta F(a, u^\star),\] and the part below it gives \[\Phi_N = \sum_{n \geq 1} (-1)^{n - 1} e^{-n m / s} \{e^{n d / s} \Delta T(-n / s; u^\star, d) - \Delta F(u^\star, d)\}.\]
  • For \(m \geq w_P\) only \(\Phi_N\) is needed, with \(u^\star = a\).

In each case \(F_{S_+}(d) = F_T(a) + \Phi / D_L\).

6.1 Truncating the series

Near the location \(x\) is close to 1 and the partial sums of the geometric series converge slowly. Each series \(\sum (-1)^n c_n\) is instead summed with weights \(W_n\) that are 1 for \(n < n_0\) and taper to 0 at \(n_0 + M\) as the upper tail of a Binomial(\(M\), 1/2). This is the Euler transform after \(n_0\) terms, the average of the partial sums from \(S_{n_0}\) to \(S_{n_0 + M}\) with binomial weights. For one \(x\) the error is \(x^{n_0} ((1 - x) / 2)^M / (1 + x)\). Every \(c_n\) is an integral of \(x^n\) over the delay density, with \(x\) in a known range, so the error of a series is at most the largest error over the range times the mass of the delay in the window. The range is \([e^{(m - w_P) / s}, e^{m / s}]\) for \(m < 0\), \([e^{-(w_P - m) / s}, 1]\) for the part above the location and \([e^{-m / s}, \min(1, e^{(w_P - m) / s})]\) for the part below it. The fewest terms, among the plain partial sum and two tapers, for which this bound is below \(10^{-10} D_L\) are used, so the error of \(F_{S_+}(d)\) is below \(10^{-10}\) of the mass of the delay in the window. It needs about 6 terms when \(x \leq 0.01\) and about 23 when the range reaches 1. The same rule is used in R and in Stan.

6.2 Admissibility

The series need the tilts up to \(\pm (n_0 + M) / s\). The exponential and gamma forms need \(\lambda - \xi > 0\) for the tilted delay to exist, which fails for the large positive tilts of a location before the end of the window unless the rate \(\lambda\) is larger than the largest tilt. The negative tilts of a location after the window always exist, so for these delays the solution applies for \(m \geq w_P\) and for a large rate. Where a tilt is not available, or no rule with at most 64 terms meets the tolerance, the methods use the numerical path, pcens_cdf.default() in R and the ODE in Stan. In Stan check_for_analytical_params() makes the choice from the parameters and the window. The normal form has no restriction.

6.3 Delays much smaller than the scale

For a delay on the non-negative reals with \(d < w_P\) and \(d / s < 10^{-4}\) equation (6.1) cancels, as only primary event times up to \(d\) contribute and \(L(p) - L(0)\) is small. With \(G_k(d) = \int_0^d (d - u)^k f_T(u) ~du\) the expansion of \(L(p) - L(0)\) in \(p\) gives \[F_{S_+}(d) = \frac{L'(0) G_1(d) + L''(0) G_2(d) / 2}{D_L} + O\big((d / s)^2\big),\] with \(L'(0) = L(0) \{1 - L(0)\} / s\) and \(L''(0) = L'(0) \{1 - 2 L(0)\} / s\). Both forms are accurate to about \(10^{-8}\) at the threshold.

6.4 Shared terms

Every transform depends on one endpoint, \(a\), \(u^\star\) or \(d\). For integer delays and an integer window the endpoints of neighbouring delays are the same integers, and so is \(u^\star = d - m\) for an integer location. The transforms are evaluated once at the unique endpoints, in pcens_pmf() and in the vectorised Stan PMFs. For a location inside the window that is not an integer each \(u^\star\) is a different point and is evaluated for its own delay.

7 Transform based solutions for a truncated Gumbel primary event time

A Gumbel window describes exposure that builds up and decays unevenly within the window. The primary event time has the Gumbel distribution with location \(\mu_G\) and scale \(\beta\) truncated to \([0, w_P]\), which is the dtgumbel() distribution. Write \(G(z) = \exp[-\exp\{-(z - \mu_G) / \beta\}]\), \(D = G(w_P) - G(0)\) and \(c(d) = \exp\{-(d - \mu_G) / \beta\}\). With \(q = d - w_P\), the reversed window on \(u \in [q, d]\) is the power series

\[ G(d - u) = \exp\{-c(d) e^{u / \beta}\} = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \frac{\{-c(d)\}^n}{n!} e^{n u / \beta}. \]

Each term is a transform at the tilt \(\xi = n / \beta\), so

\[ F_{S_+}(d) = F_T(q) + \frac{1}{D} \left[ \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \frac{\{-c(d)\}^n}{n!} \{T_f(n / \beta; d) - T_f(n / \beta; q)\} - G(0) \{F_T(d) - F_T(q)\} \right]. \tag{7.1} \]

The \(n = 0\) term is \(F_T(d) - F_T(q)\), so the package evaluates the bracket as \((1 - G(0)) \{F_T(d) - F_T(q)\}\) plus the terms with \(n \geq 1\). This keeps precision when \(\mu_G\) is far below the window and \(D\) is small. As for the exponentially tilted window, every transform depends on \(d\) or on \(q\) alone. In Stan, primarycensored_gumbel_terms() returns the transforms at every tilt for one endpoint, so primarycensored_analytical_lcdf_vectorized() computes them once per integer delay and uses them for the two windows that share the endpoint.

7.1 Where the series is accurate

The series alternates. With \(s_0 = e^{\mu_G / \beta}\), the \(n\)th term is at most \(s_0^n / n!\) times the delay mass in the window. The terms reach about \(e^{s_0}\) while the sum is of order 1, so the precision lost grows with \(s_0\). The terms are evaluated on the log scale and truncated when the bound on the next term is below \(10^{-18} \max(s_0, 1)\). The package uses the series only for \(s_0 \leq 15\), and estimates the relative error at every \(d\) from the machine precision, the sum of the absolute terms over the bracket and the truncation bound. Where it is above \(10^{-8}\) the method uses the numerical path for that \(d\). This also catches a window that is narrow relative to the scale, where the bracket is a small difference of large terms.

The numerical path integrates in a variable in which a narrow window density is smooth, because the window density is a spike of width about \(\beta\) when \(\mu_G / \beta\) is large and integration over the window can miss it. In Stan it is evaluated on the log scale, so a CDF in the far lower tail is not lost.

7.2 Admissibility

The transform is needed at the positive tilts \(n / \beta\) for \(n\) up to the number of terms. The normal delay has it at every tilt. The exponential and gamma transforms need a rate above \(N / \beta\) for \(N\) terms, which is a delay far shorter than the window, so these delays use the numerical path. In Stan check_for_gumbel_params() makes the choice from the parameters and check_for_analytical_params() uses it.
